outcome: As far as the sources I could open show, nothing has changed: no positive integer is known to be a sum of two positive fifth powers in two different ways, and no event dated on or after 26 January 2024 bears on that question (the in-window items concern a different equation, a representability question, or a polynomial analogue). Current sources, the latest dated 6 Sep 2026, still call it open.
problem_asks: Written from the statement 'Do any Taxicab(5, 2, n) exist for n > 1?' and the Wikipedia notation Taxicab(k, j, n) = the smallest number that is a sum of j positive kth powers in n different ways (Wikipedia gives k as the power and j as the number of terms, confirmed on the page). Here k = 5 (fifth powers) and j = 2 (two terms). Parts: (1) EXISTENCE: is there any positive integer N that is a sum of two positive fifth powers in n different ways for some n > 1? Equivalently, are there positive integers a, b, c, d with a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 and {a, b} different from {c, d}? (2) For each n > 1 the statement names, whether Taxicab(5,2,n) exists; the reading 'some n > 1' reduces to part (1), while the reading 'every n > 1' is stronger and is also unresolved. (3) If one exists, its value, i.e. the smallest such N for that n; the statement asks for this only conditionally on existence. Reading notes, not resolved here: 'in n different ways' can mean exactly n or at least n; the Wikipedia sidebar uses 'at least two different ways'. Summands are read as unordered and positive.

events.what_happened: Stuart Gascoigne reported an exhaustive computer search (dated Sep 2002 in an OEIS comment) finding that no solution a(5) below 3.26 x 10^32 exists, where a(5) is the smallest number expressible in two ways as a sum of two fifth powers. The figure appears in the comments of OEIS A046881, which cites a SquaresOfCubes web page for it; I did not open that page. This was a web/OEIS report, not a published paper.
events.delivers: Excludes any positive solution of a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 with two distinct representations whose common value is below 3.26 x 10^32, as reported. Says nothing at or above that value.
events.remains: Whether any solution exists at or above 3.26 x 10^32, which is the whole problem as stated.
events.time_since_posted: about 24 years (as reported, Sep 2002 to Oct 2026); the figure is only repeated in OEIS comments, not re-derived by anyone I found
events.directly_checkable: In principle, a finite search that the reader could rerun; I found no certificate or code in the sources.
events.doubts: The method and code are not described in the sources I read. The only source I found for the figure is a secondhand OEIS comment; I did not confirm it against the primary SquaresOfCubes page.
events.direction: Neither way. A finite absence of solutions below a bound is consistent with the conjecture that no solution exists and with a solution above the bound.

events.what_happened: Randy L. Ekl, 'New results in equal sums of like powers', Mathematics of Computation 67 (1998), 1309-1315 (the AMS record lists the paper). Per an OEIS A046881 comment by R. J. Mathar (7 Sep 2017), Ekl's Table 9 shows that the smallest number expressible in two ways as a sum of two fifth powers exceeds 4.01 x 10^30. I did not read the paper: the AMS page returned HTTP 403 to automated access, and the search tool gave only the listing and abstract-level metadata.
events.delivers: Lower bound only: any solution to the two-ways question exceeds 4.01 x 10^30, as reported in OEIS. No object.
events.remains: Existence of any solution, and the exact smallest value; the whole problem as stated.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for computational number theory, so the paper went through refereeing; I did not verify the refereeing record.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; I did not check whether referees engaged with the Table 9 bound specifically.

events.doubts: The 4.01 x 10^30 figure is secondhand here (OEIS comment, citing Table 9), and I could not open the table. Mathar's comment is the only source I found for it, so it is not independently confirmed in what I read.
events.direction: Neither way. A lower bound on the size of any solution.

events.what_happened: An OEIS A046881 comment by Julien Courties (2 Nov 2020) states that a(5) > 10^33, i.e. a larger lower bound than Gascoigne's 2002 figure, with no method or reference given in the comment.
events.delivers: Lower bound 10^33 on the smallest number expressible in two ways as a sum of two fifth powers, as stated in a comment with no method given.
events.remains: Existence of any solution; the whole problem as stated.
events.time_since_posted: about 6 years; the claim appears only as an OEIS comment
events.doubts: No method, search code or reference is given, so the 10^33 figure cannot be checked from what I read.

events.what_happened: An OEIS A046881 comment by Jon E. Schoenfield (15 Dec 2008) reports his own exhaustive search showing that for exponents n > 5 any solution to the two-ways question must exceed 2^96 (about 7.92 x 10^28). The same comment cites MathWorld for a(5) > 1.02 x 10^26 (MathWorld page not opened).
events.delivers: For exponents n > 5 only: any two-ways solution must exceed 2^96. Not about fifth powers, so it does not bound the exponent-5 case, though it sits in the same OEIS entry. The fifth-power figure it cites (1.02 x 10^26) is a secondhand MathWorld citation, superseded by the later bounds above.
events.doubts: The exponent-5 figure is secondhand from MathWorld and not reproduced by Schoenfield in what I read.
events.direction: Neither way; bounds for exponents above 5.

events.what_happened: OEIS A088703, 'Numbers of form x^5 + y^5, x,y > 0 and x <> y', records the conjecture 'no number can be expressed as the sum of two 5th powers in more than one way' (cross-referenced to A046881) and a search statement: 'Up to n = 100000, no instances occur where n is the sum of two distinct 5th powers in two different ways.' The sequence was submitted by Cino Hilliard on 22 Nov 2003 and edited 30 Dec 2004; the comment itself is undated. It cites Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, 2nd ed. (1994), p. 140.
events.revisions: Sequence submitted 22 Nov 2003; edited 30 Dec 2004 (per OEIS page). The conjecture and search comment are undated.
events.delivers: A conjecture (the claim the problem asks about, stated as a negative answer) plus a search over values up to 100000, which is a trivially small finite search. Neither establishes or moves anything about existence.
events.time_since_posted: about 22 years; the conjecture is restated in the OEIS entry without any cited verification
events.doubts: A conjecture that matches the open question is not evidence about it. The search bound (100000) is far below the known lower bounds, so it adds nothing.
events.direction: Neither way; it states the expected negative answer as a conjecture and checks a tiny range.

events.what_happened: L. J. Lander and T. R. Parkin, 'Counterexample to Euler's Conjecture on Sums of Like Powers', Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 72 (1966), 1079, communicated 27 June 1966 (per the AMS record). It reports a direct CDC 6600 search finding 27^5 + 84^5 + 110^5 + 133^5 = 144^5: four fifth powers summing to a fifth power. This is a five-term equation, not a two-term one, and it does not bear on the sum-of-two-fifth-powers question. I checked the identity by hand (both sides equal 61,917,364,224). The AMS record was seen in search results only and not opened.
events.delivers: Disproves Euler's conjecture for fifth powers: four fifth powers can sum to a fifth power. Establishes nothing about a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 (two terms, two representations).
events.remains: Everything the problem asks; this is a neighbouring result (different equation, different number of terms).

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the AMS, refereed journal
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; refereeing applies to the note as published.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the note; I did not verify the refereeing record.

events.directly_checkable: The identity 27^5 + 84^5 + 110^5 + 133^5 = 144^5 can be checked by computing both sides; I did so by hand (61,917,364,224 each side).
events.doubts: A secondary source prints 25^5 for 27^5, a typo; the AMS original should be used. Nothing else.
events.direction: Neither way for this problem; it is a counterexample to a different conjecture (Euler's, with four terms on one side). It is the lead fifth-power search result and is discounted for this problem.
events.object: The identity 27^5 + 84^5 + 110^5 + 133^5 = 144^5 with 4 fifth powers on one side and 1 on the other, found by direct computer search (explicit, not an existence proof).

events.what_happened: Geoffrey B. Campbell and Aleksander Zujev, 'Gaussian integer solutions for the fifth power taxicab number problem', arXiv:1511.07424, submitted 21 Nov 2015 (single version). The paper calls the positive-integer case of a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 a famous open problem and gives infinite families of solutions when some variables are Gaussian integers: a mixed family (a, b integers, c, d Gaussian) built from Pell numbers, and an all-Gaussian family. Example: 3^5 + 1^5 = (2+3i)^5 + (2-3i)^5, which I checked by hand ((2+3i)^5 + (2-3i)^5 = 244 = 243 + 1).
events.revisions: v1 only (21 Nov 2015), per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Infinite families of solutions to a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 in which some or all of the four variables are Gaussian integers. Establishes nothing for positive integers; the restriction to Gaussian integers is the whole content and the paper does not claim a positive-integer solution.
events.remains: Existence of any positive-integer solution with two representations, which is the problem's core question, and every other part of the problem.
events.time_since_posted: about 10 years 10 months; I found no follow-up that verifies or extends the Gaussian families, but I did not search citing works in zbMATH or Google Scholar
events.directly_checkable: The Gaussian identities can be checked by expanding powers; the example above checks by hand.
events.direction: Cuts toward existence only in the Gaussian-integer setting. For positive integers it neither confirms nor refutes existence; the paper itself presents the integer case as open.
events.object: Infinite families indexed by Pell numbers, explicit: a mixed family with a, b positive integers and c, d Gaussian integers, plus an all-Gaussian family. The first member is 3^5 + 1^5 = (2+3i)^5 + (2-3i)^5. Explicit construction, not an existence proof. The all-Gaussian family was seen only in search excerpts, not in full.

events.what_happened: Brennan Benfield, Oliver Lippard and Arindam Roy, 'End Behavior of Ramanujan's Taxicab Numbers', arXiv:2404.08190 (submitted 12 Apr 2024). The paper studies Taxicab(k, j, m) as the number of summands j grows, with examples such as no positive integer being a sum of exactly 10 positive squares in exactly 3 ways. It is about a different parameter regime and does not settle Taxicab(5,2,n). Its introduction restates the fifth-power two-term case as open: 'Taxicab(5,2,2) is unknown', citing Calude, Calude and Dinneen, and it says 'It could be that no such number exists.' Section 7 says 'it is unknown [12] if the equation A^k+B^k=C^k+D^k has solutions for k>4', citing Ekl.
events.revisions: v1 12 Apr 2024 (arXiv stamp). OEIS A393788 cites the paper as published in The Ramanujan Journal 66(1) (2025); the journal version was not opened.
events.delivers: Nothing on Taxicab(5,2,n). It restates the problem as open and gives general results for large j and squares with ways m; its fifth-power content is the restatement and the remark that no such number may exist.
events.remains: Everything the problem asks; the paper leaves Taxicab(5,2,2) explicitly unknown.

checked_by.who: The Ramanujan Journal, refereed journal (the paper's published venue per OEIS A393788)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; it refereed the paper's own results, not the Taxicab(5,2,2) remark.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; I did not verify the refereeing record.

events.direction: Neither way for this problem. It restates the problem as open and says a nonexistence answer is possible.

events.what_happened: Brennan Benfield and Oliver Lippard, 'Integers that are not the sum of positive powers', arXiv:2404.08193 (submitted 12 Apr 2024; v2 31 Mar 2025). It asks which positive integers cannot be written as a sum of j positive kth powers and gives computations for 5 <= k <= 9, so it covers fifth powers. It is a representability question (non-representable integers), not a multiplicity question (two representations), and the abstract does not mention taxicab numbers or Taxicab(5,2,n).
events.revisions: v1 12 Apr 2024; v2 31 Mar 2025 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Results on which integers are not sums of j positive kth powers for 5 <= k <= 9. Settles nothing about whether a number has two representations as a sum of two fifth powers; it asks a different question about the same sums.
events.time_since_posted: about 2.5 years; no engagement found in my searches
events.direction: Neither way for this problem; a representability result on a different question about the same sums.

events.what_happened: Jeffrey M. Braun, 'The fourth known primitive solution to a^5 + b^5 + c^5 + d^5 = e^5', arXiv:2603.05549, v1 submitted 5 Mar 2026. The abstract reports a new primitive solution to a four-term-plus-one equation with target e = 1,956,878, found by a large-scale computational search with an optimized meet-in-the-middle algorithm. It is about a different equation (four fifth powers on the left, one on the right) and does not concern a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 or Taxicab numbers.
events.revisions: v1 5 Mar 2026; v2 21 Apr 2026; v3 19 Aug 2026; v4 21 Aug 2026 (listing comment: 'Updated author metadata'). The content of v2 and v3 was not compared against v1.
events.delivers: A new primitive solution to a^5 + b^5 + c^5 + d^5 = e^5 (the fourth known one). Establishes nothing about a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 (two terms on one side).
events.time_since_posted: about 7 months; no public engagement found in my searches
events.directly_checkable: The solution can be checked by computing both sides. I did not compute it. From a search-tool text extraction (not the abstract, and not checked by me), the bases are 719115, 1331622, -1340632, 1956213 with e = 1956878; check against the PDF before relying on it.
events.direction: Neither way for this problem. It is a counterexample-type result for Euler's sum-of-powers conjecture with a different number of terms.
events.object: A primitive solution to a^5 + b^5 + c^5 + d^5 = e^5 with e = 1,956,878 (from the abstract), one base negative (bases as in the directly_checkable note, not verified by me). It is explicit and was found by search, not by a non-constructive argument.

ai.disclosed_cost: A search-tool excerpt reports about 10,500,000 vCPU-hours. I did not see this in the abstract and did not verify it in the paper.

events.what_happened: Katalin Gyarmati, 'Ramanujan, the taxicab problem for polynomials, and the abc-conjecture', arXiv:2604.25017 (v1 27 Apr 2026). The abstract studies whether equations p^n + q^n = r^n + s^n, and more general sums of powers equal to zero, have solutions among polynomials. It is a polynomial analogue. A search snippet gives the journal version as Research in Number Theory 12(9) (2026), DOI 10.1007/s40993-026-00699-1, which I did not open.
events.revisions: v1 27 Apr 2026 (per the arXiv abstract page); journal version per search snippet.
events.delivers: Results about polynomial solutions to the taxicab-type equations. An analogue, not the integer question, so it does not settle or move the integer problem.
events.remains: Everything the problem asks, over the integers.

checked_by.who: Research in Number Theory (Springer), refereed journal, per search snippet
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the polynomial result.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; not opened and not verified.

events.direction: Neither way for this problem. It is a polynomial analogue, which the problem does not ask about.

summary: Nothing I could open shows that any Taxicab(5,2,n) with n >= 2 exists or that none does, and the problem is still listed as open. The Wikipedia article on generalized taxicab numbers (opened) says Taxicab(5,2,n) is 'not known for any n >= 2' and that 'it is not known whether such a number exists', citing only Guy's book. The AMS Math Grad blog post by Avery Carr (opened, dated 15 Aug 2013) says 'no one knows what the general taxicab number, Taxicab(5,2,n), equals for any n > 1' and 'so far, all attempts to prove the weaker version have failed.' The a3nm survey post (opened; the fetch tool gave its date as 6 Sep 2026) still says 'We also do not know whether for p=5 we could have l=k=2.' The Wikipedia Lander-Parkin-Selfridge article (opened; last edited 14 Sep 2026 per the fetch tool) says no nontrivial positive-integer solution of a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 is known, citing Kiss and Sandor (2022), which I did not open. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 onward) I found four items, all discounted under section 2.1: Benfield-Lippard-Roy 2024 (large-j Taxicab numbers, which restates the case as open), Benfield-Lippard 2024 (a representability question for 5 <= k <= 9), Braun March 2026 (a four-term fifth-power equation) and Gyarmati April 2026 (a polynomial analogue). The pre-window events are bounds and one Gaussian-integer result: Gascoigne's 2002 search finding no solution below 3.26 x 10^32; Ekl's 1998 bound 4.01 x 10^30 (secondhand, Table 9 not read); Courties' 2020 comment a(5) > 10^33 (no method given); Campbell and Zujev's 2015 Gaussian-integer families (explicit, but they leave the integer case open). Each is recorded separately. Close calls: (a) Ekl and Courties bound the smallest value of the very quantity the problem names (Taxicab(5,2,2)), which is the kind of bound section 2.1 says can move a named quantity; I have discounted them because they are finite lower bounds that leave existence open. (b) Benfield et al. 2024 report the same question as open in their introduction (citing Calude et al. and Ekl), which I recorded as a later-work restatement rather than an event on the question. Parameterisation traps, all discounted: the OEIS 'five positive squares in exactly two ways is 20' result (search excerpt) is Taxicab(2,5,2), and the 'no number is a sum of 10 squares in 3 ways' result is Taxicab(2,10,3); both are different problems. The 2008 Emelyanov paper (arXiv:0802.1147) concerns cubes (k=3). AI involvement: I searched explicitly for AI with taxicab numbers, fifth powers and two-term Diophantine equations and found no report of any AI system bearing on this problem. The 2026 AI counterexample work I checked (the 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' paper, whose introduction lists ten AI-disproved conjectures, none in this area) and Grechuk's Diophantine list (ChatGPT credited for other equations, seen in search excerpts) concern other problems. For each event, ai.none_found is true because the source names no system; the Braun paper names a computational search, not AI. Two readings of the question were left open and both are recorded in the problem_asks field: 'in n different ways' as exactly n or at least n, and 'Do any exist for n > 1' as 'for some n' or 'for every n'. The 'some n' reading reduces to whether any positive integer has two representations.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the bounds differently: Taxicab(5,2,2) is the named quantity, and Gascoigne's 3.26 x 10^32, Ekl's 4.01 x 10^30 and Courties' 10^33 are lower bounds on it. On section 2.1's test (a quantity named in the statement moved), a judge could count these as moving the problem, not as finite checks. The case against is that the statement asks about existence and the bounds do not decide it; a lower bound pushed up by a finite search leaves existence open, the same way Collatz verifications do. A second, stronger reading comes from the conjecture landscape: the Lander-Parkin-Selfridge conjecture predicts that equal sums with fewer than k terms in total have no solution, and for k = 5 the (5,2,2) type has 4 < 5 terms, so LPS predicts the answer is no. The Wikipedia LPS article states that (5,2,2) is one of the two possible counterexample types for k = 5 and that neither is known to have a solution. That is a reason to expect a negative answer, not evidence about the sources, so it belongs to the judging pass.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit pair of positive-integer representations a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 with {a,b} different from {c,d} (checkable by computing both sides, which would settle the existence question for n = 2 at once), or a proof that none exists, which would also resolve the (5,2,2) case of the Lander-Parkin-Selfridge conjecture. For the bounds, the primary Ekl 1998 Table 9 (AMS page refused automated access; the paper itself was not read) would confirm the 4.01 x 10^30 figure, the SquaresOfCubes page would confirm Gascoigne's 2002 search, and a method note from the 2020 OEIS comment would confirm the 10^33 bound.
